_about: Real cooking tips and dish facts shown in the corner of a close-up while you cook (CookSession). By recipe id (data/recipes/<id>.tres): 'steps' are tips for one step (by its exact title), shown while that step is going; 'facts' are about the dish, shown on any step without a tip of its own, one after another.

steps.Whisk the batter: Don't over-mix pancake batter: a few lumps are fine. Mixing too much builds gluten and makes pancakes tough instead of fluffy.
steps.Flip them: Flip when bubbles on top pop and stay open, and the edges look dry: that means the bottom has set.

facts: Honey never really goes off: pots of it found in ancient Egyptian tombs were still edible.
The first pancake often comes out pale because the pan isn't evenly hot yet. Chefs call it the 'test pancake'.

steps.Butter the griddle: Butter browns and burns at a lower heat than oil. For a hot griddle, a little oil with the butter helps stop it scorching.
steps.Crack the eggs: Never crack an egg on the edge of a bowl: it pushes bits of shell into the egg. Crack it on a flat surface instead.
steps.Lay the bacon: Lay bacon strips away from you, so any hot fat that spits goes away from you too.
steps.Flip the bacon: Bacon curls because the fat and the meat shrink by different amounts as they cook. Turning it now and then helps it stay flat.
steps.Ketchup smile: In the 1830s, tomato ketchup was even sold as a medicine, in pill form.

facts: Sunny-side-up eggs are never flipped: the top sets from the heat rising through the egg.

steps.Pour the eggs: Beat eggs until no streaks of white are left, so the omelette comes out an even yellow.
steps.Fold it in half: Take the omelette off the heat while the middle is still a little soft: it keeps cooking on its own.

facts: Omurice is a Japanese dish from the early 1900s: an omelette wrapped round or laid over ketchup fried rice.
In Japan, omurice is often decorated with a ketchup message or drawing on top.

steps.Press them flat: Pressing hotteok flat spreads the sugar filling to the edges and crisps the outside.

facts: Hotteok is a Korean street-food pancake. Its brown sugar, cinnamon and nut filling melts into syrup as it cooks.
Careful with the first bite of hotteok: the melted sugar inside is much hotter than the outside.

steps.Pipe the dough: Churros are piped through a star-shaped tip. The ridges help them cook evenly and stop them bursting in the hot oil.
steps.Chocolate: In Spain, churros are often dunked in hot chocolate thick enough to coat them.

facts: Churros are thought to come from Spain and Portugal, and are now loved all over Latin America.

steps.Roll the crust: Keep pie dough cold. Little pieces of butter melt in the oven, and the steam they give off lifts the crust into flaky layers.
steps.Lattice top: A lattice top lets steam escape, so the fruit filling thickens instead of turning soupy.

facts: A pie needs to cool for a few hours before slicing, or the hot filling runs out.

steps.Roll the dough: Chill cookie dough before rolling and cutting: cold dough keeps its shape in the oven.
steps.Bake: Cookies keep cooking on the hot tray after they come out, so take them out when the edges are just golden.

facts: Real acorns are very bitter. People who eat them soak them in water first to wash the bitterness out.

steps.Fill with custard: Fill the tart cases just short of the top: the custard puffs up a little as it bakes.

facts: Portuguese custard tarts (pastéis de nata) inspired the egg tarts of Macau and Hong Kong.
The dark spots on top of an egg tart come from the custard's sugar caramelising in a very hot oven.

steps.Roll the pastry thin: Traditional strudel dough is stretched so thin you could read a newspaper through it.

facts: Apple strudel is a classic of Vienna, Austria. The oldest known strudel recipe is from 1696.

steps.Fold in thirds: Every fold multiplies the layers of butter and dough. After a few folds there are dozens of them; rolled and shaped, they make a croissant's flakes.
steps.Turn it: Keep the dough cold between folds, so the butter stays in its own layer instead of melting into the dough.
steps.Bake: In the oven, the water in the butter turns to steam and puffs the thin layers apart.

facts: Croissants are famously French, but they grew out of the Austrian kipferl, a crescent-shaped bread.

steps.Twist them: Legend says monks first twisted pretzels to look like arms folded in prayer.
steps.Stir in the milk: Add milk to a cheese sauce a little at a time and keep stirring, so it stays smooth.
steps.Stir until smooth: Keep cheese sauce on low heat. Too hot and the cheese turns stringy or grainy.

facts: Pretzels get their deep brown shine from a quick dip in an alkaline bath, like baking-soda water, before baking.

steps.Whisk until smooth: Whisk out every lump before cooking the mochi: lumps don't cook out.
steps.Dust the counter: Dust the counter with starch or powdered sugar, or the mochi sticks to everything.

facts: Mochi is made from glutinous rice, which has no gluten at all: 'glutinous' just means sticky.
In Japan, mochi is traditionally made at New Year by pounding steamed rice with a big wooden mallet.

steps.Pleat them shut: Pleating gathers the wrapper so it hugs the filling and seals tight.
steps.Steam them: Steam dumplings on a liner, like cabbage leaves or baking paper, so they don't stick.

facts: In China, dumplings are eaten at Lunar New Year: their shape is said to look like old gold ingots, for good luck.

steps.Chili oil: Chili heat comes from capsaicin, which dissolves in fat, not water. That's why chili oil carries the heat so well.

facts: Too spicy? Milk helps more than water: a protein in milk breaks up capsaicin and washes it away.

steps.Boil the pasta: Al dente is Italian for 'to the tooth': cooked, but still a little firm when you bite it.
steps.Drain it: Save a little of the cloudy pasta water: the starch in it helps a cheese sauce turn silky instead of clumping.
steps.Grate the cheese: Grate cheese yourself: ready-grated cheese is coated in starch so it doesn't clump, which can make a sauce grainy.

facts: Mixing cheeses works well: some melt smoothly, like cheddar, and others bring lots of flavour, like parmesan.

steps.Arrange the greens: Make sure salad leaves are dry, or the dressing slides right off them.
steps.Whip on the foam: Chefs often make foams with soy lecithin, which holds tiny air bubbles in place.
steps.Vinaigrette: Dress a salad just before serving: salt and vinegar pull water out of the leaves and make them wilt.

steps.Stir: Stir soup from the bottom of the pot, so nothing catches and burns.
steps.Season to taste: Season a soup near the end: as it simmers, water boils off and it gets saltier on its own.

facts: Cut soup vegetables to the same size so they all finish cooking at the same time.
Simmer soup gently: a hard boil turns vegetables mushy and the broth cloudy.

steps.Into the pot: Fish cooks in just a few minutes. Add it near the end, or it falls apart in the stew.
steps.Season: salt: Season a little at a time and taste as you go: you can add more salt, but you can't take it out.

steps.Peel: Peel away from yourself, so the peeler can't slip toward your hand.
steps.Chop: Curl the fingertips of the hand holding the food under, like a claw, so the knife can't reach them.

facts: A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one: it needs less force, so it's less likely to slip.

steps.Peel the carrot: Peel away from yourself, so the peeler can't slip toward your hand.
steps.Skin the onion: Cutting an onion lets out a gas that stings your eyes. A sharp knife crushes fewer cells, so there are fewer tears.
steps.Chop the carrot: Curl the fingertips of the hand holding the food under, like a claw, so the knife can't reach them.

facts: Onions turn sweet as they cook: heat drives off the sharp flavor and leaves the sugars.
A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one: it needs less force, so it's less likely to slip.
A fillet knife is thin and bendy, so it can follow the fish's bones and leave less fish behind.
Fish often bite best around dawn and dusk, when the light is low and lots of insects are out.
Wash the cleanest things first, like glasses, then plates, then greasy pans, so the water stays cleaner for longer.
Pat steak dry before searing: a wet surface steams instead of browning.
The brown crust on a seared steak is the Maillard reaction: proteins and sugars browning at around 140 °C (285 °F) and up.
Searing doesn't really seal in a steak's juices. What it adds is flavour, from all that browning.
Let a steak rest for a few minutes after cooking, so its juices settle before you cut it.
